bmo-bmo1-2024-01.title: Place the letters one at a time
bmo-bmo1-2024-01.body:
"At most one letter late" means: the $j$-th letter of the word is typed in one of the positions $1,2,\dots,j+1$.

Place the letters of OLYMPIADS in order, $j=1,2,\dots,9$.
- O (the 1st letter) goes in position $1$ or $2$: $2$ choices.
- For $2\le j\le8$: the $j$-th letter must go in one of the positions $1,\dots,j+1$. Exactly $j-1$ of these are already taken by the first $j-1$ letters (all of which sit in positions $\le j$), so exactly $2$ positions remain: $2$ choices.
- The final S goes into the one position that is left. This is allowed, since every position is $\le 10$.

Every sequence of choices gives a different valid spelling, and every valid spelling arises this way. So the number of spellings is $2^8=256$.

**Answer: 256.** ∎

*(Note: there are only $8$ independent choices, not $9$ — the last letter is forced. $512$ is a common wrong answer.)*

bmo-bmo1-2024-01.title: Recursion on the word length
bmo-bmo1-2024-01.body:
Let $f(n)$ be the number of valid spellings of an $n$-letter word with distinct letters; $f(1)=1$.

Take a word $L_1L_2\cdots L_n$ with $n\ge2$. In the shorter word $L_2\cdots L_n$ the letter $L_k$ has index $k-1$, so "valid" there means $L_k$ is in position $\le k$.
- In a valid spelling of the long word, $L_1$ is in position $1$ or $2$. Deleting it gives a valid spelling of $L_2\cdots L_n$: a letter $L_k$ ($k\ge2$) after $L_1$ moves from position $\le k+1$ to $\le k$, and a letter before $L_1$ is in position $1\le k$.
- Conversely, inserting $L_1$ in position $1$ or $2$ into a valid spelling of $L_2\cdots L_n$ moves every other letter right by at most one place, so $L_k$ ends in position $\le k+1$: valid.

These two insertions give different spellings, and different shorter spellings give different results.

Hence $f(n)=2f(n-1)$, so $f(n)=2^{n-1}$ and $f(9)=2^8=256$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-02.title: Differences never shrink
bmo-bmo1-2024-02.body:
Let $d_i=a_i-a_{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$.
- If $a_i=2a_{i-1}-a_{i-2}$, then $d_i=a_{i-1}-a_{i-2}=d_{i-1}$.
- If $a_i=2a_{i-2}-a_{i-1}$, then $d_i=2a_{i-2}-2a_{i-1}=-2d_{i-1}$.

Either way $|d_i|\ge|d_{i-1}|$, and if $d_{i-1}=0$ then $d_i=0$.

If $d_1=0$, then all $d_i=0$ and $a_{2024}=a_{2023}$, which is not the case. So $d_1$ is a nonzero integer and
$$1\le|d_1|\le|d_2|\le\dots\le|d_{2024}|=1 .$$
Hence $|a_1-a_0|=|d_1|=1$: $a_0$ and $a_1$ are consecutive. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-02.title: Backward induction
bmo-bmo1-2024-02.body:
We show: if $a_i$ and $a_{i+1}$ are consecutive ($i\ge1$), then so are $a_{i-1}$ and $a_i$. Then, starting from $a_{2023},a_{2024}$ and stepping down, $a_0,a_1$ are consecutive.

Suppose $a_{i+1}=a_i+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon=\pm1$.
- If $a_{i+1}=2a_i-a_{i-1}$, then $a_{i-1}=2a_i-a_{i+1}=a_i-\varepsilon$, consecutive with $a_i$.
- If $a_{i+1}=2a_{i-1}-a_i$, then $a_{i-1}=\frac{a_i+a_{i+1}}2=a_i+\frac\varepsilon2$, not an integer — impossible.

So $a_{i-1}=a_i-\varepsilon$, which is consecutive with $a_i$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-03.title: Two circles: the circumcircle and the circle centred at B
bmo-bmo1-2024-03.body:
**Configuration.** Since $\angle BAC<90^\circ$ and $\angle BCA<\angle BAC$, the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ lies inside $AC$ and $X$, the reflection of $A$ in that foot, lies inside segment $AC$. In an accurate figure $Y$ lies on arc $BC$ on $B$'s side of $AC$, $X$ lies between $Y$ and $Z$, and $Z$ lies on the arc $AC$ not containing $B$. Let $\omega$ be the circle with centre $B$ and radius $BA$; it passes through $A$, $X$ and $Y$.

Let $\theta=\angle ZBA$.
1. **Angles in the same segment** (circle $ABC$, chord $AZ$, with $B$ and $Y$ on the same side): $\angle ZYA=\angle ZBA=\theta$.
2. Since $X$ lies on segment $YZ$, $\angle XYA=\angle ZYA=\theta$.
3. **Angle at the centre** (circle $\omega$, chord $AX$; $Y$ on the major arc, on the same side of $AX$ as the centre $B$): $\angle XBA=2\angle XYA=2\theta$.

So $\angle XBZ=\angle XBA-\angle ZBA=\theta=\angle ZBA$: line $BZ$ is the bisector of the apex angle of the isosceles triangle $XBA$ ($BX=BA$). In an isosceles triangle this bisector is perpendicular to the base, so $BZ\perp XA$, i.e. $BZ\perp AC$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-03.title: Show ZA = ZX (a kite)
bmo-bmo1-2024-03.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle BAC$ and $\delta=\angle XYB$ (configuration as in the first solution).
- $BX=BY$: in triangle $XBY$, $\angle BXY=\delta$.
- $BX=BA$: in triangle $ABX$, $\angle AXB=\alpha$.
- $Y,X,Z$ are collinear: $\angle ZXA=180^\circ-\angle YXB-\angle BXA=180^\circ-\delta-\alpha$.
- $ABYZ$ is a cyclic quadrilateral (vertices in this order), so $\angle BAZ=180^\circ-\angle BYZ=180^\circ-\delta$, hence $\angle XAZ=\angle BAZ-\angle BAX=180^\circ-\delta-\alpha$.

So triangle $XZA$ has equal angles at $X$ and $A$, and $ZA=ZX$. Now $B$ and $Z$ are both equidistant from $A$ and $X$, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AX$; thus $BZ$ is that perpendicular bisector and $BZ\perp AX=AC$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-04.title: Factor a² − 1 and bound
bmo-bmo1-2024-04.body:
Suppose $n\cdot2^n+1=a^2$ with $a>0$, so $(a-1)(a+1)=n\cdot2^n$.

The right side is even, so $a$ is odd and $a-1$, $a+1$ are consecutive even numbers; one of them is $2\times$(odd). The product contains at least $n$ factors of $2$, so the **other** factor, call it $u$, is divisible by $2^{n-1}$. Let $v$ be the factor that is $2\times$ odd. Then $uv=n2^n$ with $u\ge2^{n-1}$, so $v\le 2n$, and since $u$ and $v$ differ by $2$,
$$2^{n-1}\le u\le v+2\le2n+2 .$$

This fails for $n\ge5$: for $n=5$, $2^4=16>12$; and if $2^{k-1}>2k+2$ then $2^k>4k+4>2(k+1)+2$. So $n\le4$.

Check: $n=1$: $3$ (no); $n=2$: $9=3^2$ (yes); $n=3$: $25=5^2$ (yes); $n=4$: $65$ (no).

**Answer:** $n=2$ and $n=3$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-05.title: RRBB pattern and overlapping blocks of five
bmo-bmo1-2024-05.body:
**250 is achievable.** Colour the dots $RRBB\,RRBB\ldots$ (the pattern fits since $4\mid1000$). Each $RR$ pair is one fault — $250$ faults. Each blue dot is two places from a red dot on both sides ($B$ at positions $\equiv3,0\pmod4$ are two away from positions $\equiv1,2$), so there are no blue faults. Total: $250$.

**At least 250 in any colouring.** *Every five consecutive dots $d_1,\dots,d_5$ contain a fault (both dots of the fault among them).* If one of $d_2,d_3,d_4$ is red, either it has a red neighbour (a red fault) or both its neighbours are blue, and those two are two apart (a blue fault). If none of $d_2,d_3,d_4$ is red, then $d_2,d_4$ are blue and two apart.

Number the dots $1,\dots,1000$ and take the $250$ blocks $\{4j-3,\dots,4j+1\}$ for $j=1,\dots,250$ (the last block is $997,\dots,1000,1$). Two different blocks share at most one dot, while a fault consists of two dots; so a fault lies in at most one block. Each block contains a fault, so there are at least $250$ faults.

**Answer: 250.** ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-05.title: Non-overlapping blocks of four
bmo-bmo1-2024-05.body:
The construction $RRBB\ldots$ gives $250$ faults, as in the first solution.

**The only fault-free string of four dots is $RBBR$.** If the first dot is $R$, the second is $B$ (no $RR$), then the fourth is $R$ (no $B\_B$ with the second), then the third is $B$ (no $RR$). If the first is $B$, the third is $R$, so the second and fourth are $B$ — a blue fault.

Split the circle into $250$ disjoint blocks of four consecutive dots. For each fault $\{i,i+1\}$ or $\{i,i+2\}$, call dot $i$ its *first* dot. Each block contains the first dot of some fault:
- if the block contains a fault, that fault's first dot is in the block;
- if the block is $RBBR$, look at the next dot: if it is red, it forms a red fault with the block's last dot; if blue, it forms a blue fault with the block's third dot. Either way the fault's first dot is in the block.

Different blocks give faults with different first dots, hence different faults: at least $250$. **Answer: 250.** ∎

bmo-bmo1-2024-06.title: Angles two apart are equal; a counterexample for even n
bmo-bmo1-2024-06.body:
Indices are taken mod $n$; call the common edge length *edge* and the common length of the diagonals $v_iv_{i+3}$ *$d$*.

**Odd $n$: the polygon is equiangular.** Fix $i$ and look at $v_i,v_{i+1},v_{i+2},v_{i+3},v_{i+4}$ (distinct, as $n\ge5$).
- Triangles $v_iv_{i+1}v_{i+3}$ and $v_{i+4}v_{i+3}v_{i+1}$ have sides (edge, $v_{i+1}v_{i+3}$, $d$) and (edge, $v_{i+3}v_{i+1}$, $d$), so they are congruent (SSS), with $v_i\leftrightarrow v_{i+4}$, $v_{i+1}\leftrightarrow v_{i+3}$. Hence $\angle v_iv_{i+1}v_{i+3}=\angle v_{i+4}v_{i+3}v_{i+1}=:\beta$.
- Triangle $v_{i+1}v_{i+2}v_{i+3}$ is isosceles (two edges), so $\angle v_{i+2}v_{i+1}v_{i+3}=\angle v_{i+2}v_{i+3}v_{i+1}=:\alpha$.
- In a convex polygon the diagonal $v_{i+1}v_{i+3}$ lies inside the angles of the polygon at $v_{i+1}$ and at $v_{i+3}$. So the polygon's angle at $v_{i+1}$ is $\beta+\alpha$, and so is its angle at $v_{i+3}$.

Thus the angles at $v_{j}$ and $v_{j+2}$ are equal for every $j$. When $n$ is odd, stepping by $2$ visits every vertex ($v_1,v_3,\dots,v_n,v_2,v_4,\dots$), so all angles are equal.

**Even $n=2k$ ($k\ge3$): a non-equiangular example.** Start with a regular $k$-gon of side $s$, and on each side erect externally an isosceles triangle with base angles $\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<\frac{90^\circ}{k}$. The $k$ apexes and the $k$ original vertices, alternately, form a $2k$-gon.
- *Equilateral:* every edge is a leg of one of the congruent isosceles triangles.
- *Convex:* angle at an apex $=180^\circ-2\alpha<180^\circ$; angle at an original vertex $=\bigl(180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{k}\bigr)+2\alpha<180^\circ$ because $\alpha<\frac{180^\circ}k$.
- *Not equiangular:* the two angles are equal only if $\alpha=\frac{90^\circ}{k}$, which we excluded.
- *Equal diagonals:* of $v_i,v_{i+3}$ one is an apex and one an original vertex. If $v_i$ is an apex, triangle $v_iv_{i+1}v_{i+3}$ has sides leg $v_iv_{i+1}$ and $k$-gon side $v_{i+1}v_{i+3}=s$ with included angle $\alpha+\bigl(180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}k\bigr)$. If $v_i$ is an original vertex, triangle $v_iv_{i+2}v_{i+3}$ has sides $s$ and a leg with the same included angle at $v_{i+2}$. By SAS all these triangles are congruent, so all diagonals $v_iv_{i+3}$ are equal.

**Answer:** the polygon must be equiangular exactly when $n$ is odd. ∎
